title: Tuppence and the Mysterious Footprints
markdown:
The Great Grey Peaks of Whisperwind stood like sleeping giants in mist that could not decide whether to dance or sit. In the valleys, waterfalls were silver ribbon and stairs were cut into cliff. Tuppence the ogre was not a grumble. He was a summer-breeze sort of large, hands good at shy herbs. Button, a plump hen, punctuated his days with clucks that meant yes, no, and beetle.

One apple-tasting morning, mist still deciding the valley’s edges, he was with the prize moonpetal mint—silver leaves, sleepy scent, the plant that had won a ribbon he kept in a drawer because ribbons made Button try to eat them—when he saw them: footprints, boot-wobbly, far bigger than hen, pressed by the thyme and the rosemary too, a dent in the nasturtiums as if someone had paused to be polite and then forgotten how.

“Peculiar,” he said. Button pecked a print, thoughtful. “Someone has been tiptoeing my seasoning.”

Fidget arrived in emerald rustle, grin that could outwit a magpie. “Mysterious! Grand! Surprising!” Pebble-cackle. Tuppence found him dizzying and nodded anyway. “I want the nasturtium thief.”

Toward the whispering woods a lute found them. Lyra the elf musician turned Tuppence into a ballad before he had finished his sentence. “Gentle heart! Giant footprints! Quest!”

“Petunias,” Tuppence said. Button had left after a rainbow beetle.

The trail passed a waterfall that roared like a dragon between naps, spray making a second weather, then worn stone stairs that remembered other feet, moss in velvet patches you wanted to apologise to. Lyra sang ravines and standing stones and legendary pursuit until even the echo sounded tired of being famous. “Button,” Tuppence asked, “is this the right beetle, or a dramatic one?” She bawkked, which could have meant either, and nudged him onto a moss bridge over a gorge that kept its water as an argument and its shadows as a hobby. The handrail was a suggestion. Tuppence took it anyway, because large people who are gentle still fall if they are proud.

Under the arch, glow-worms pulsed emerald, a living underside of stars. More prints. Fragments of woven grass. A scent of dew-clover and hay: the same breath that had visited his beds.

He looked at Button, who pecked a loose stone. It scraped aside on a small dark hole. “If you are going to be mysterious,” Tuppence told the mountain, “a note would help.” Lyra’s lute sighed, almost embarrassed.

Inside, in worm-light, a shy creature: twilight fur, grey with a hint of purple, eyes holding moon. A grass bundle. Trembling. The feet, afraid of day. Button clucked comfort and pushed Tuppence’s hand toward kindness.

Flicker, a Twilight Weaver, lost, a being of quiet shadows, loud-noises-averse, night-raiding herbs and trying not to exist too loudly. The garden had smelled like a welcome. Fidget, for once, shut up, which was a kind of respect.

Tuppence coaxed as he coaxed mint. Large hands, for growing. Button shared seeds. Fidget, surprising himself, sketched a path to a hidden meadow far from songs that named people legendary. Lyra played smaller. They watched Flicker go, a grey-purple comma becoming distance. Chamomile weather settled on the three of them. The mist on the peaks softened, as mist does when nobody is asking it to be epic.
characters: Tuppence (ogre Tuppence), Button (hen Button), Fidget (goblin Fidget)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
